6 questions — Name the tactic in the message and the adversary behind the incident (CED Topic 2.1, EK 2.1.A–B)

column4: >Predict the tactic or adversary type before you look at the options

column1: Read the Message, Then Name the Adversary

EK 2.1.A lists the tactics an adversary uses to manipulate a target — authority, urgency, scarcity, consensus, familiarity, intimidation, and pretexting. EK 2.1.B lists who is doing the manipulating — script kiddies, hacktivists, insider adversaries, cyberterrorists, and transnational criminal organizations.

Questions 1, 2 and 6 hand you a message and ask for the tactic. Questions 3 and 4 hand you an incident and ask for the adversary type. Question 5 asks you to find the one definition that is stated wrongly. Write your answer down before you read the choices: every distractor here is a real tactic or a real adversary type, so an option sounding plausible is not evidence that it is right.

Message received: “This is Dana in the CFO’s office. He needs the vendor payment file in the next 20 minutes or the quarterly close gets flagged by the auditors.” Predict the tactics before you read the choices. Which pair BEST describes what the sender is using?

Relaying instructions that come from someone with power over the target is authority (EK 2.1.A.3), and a 20-minute deadline framed as averting a bad outcome is urgency (EK 2.1.A.8). Both arrive in one short message, which is exactly how real payment-fraud calls are built.
(B) Incorrect — nothing in the message limits the supply of a resource (scarcity) or claims that other employees have already complied (consensus).

(C) Incorrect — the sender never claims a personal relationship with the target (familiarity), and an audit flag on the quarterly close is a business consequence, not a threat of harm to the target (intimidation).
(D) Incorrect — “Dana in the CFO’s office” is a pretext, so half of this pair is defensible, but the message makes no appeal to what other people are doing.
Exam Tip: When two tactics show up together, separate who is applying the pressure from how the pressure is shaped. Authority answers the first
column2: urgency, scarcity, and intimidation answer the second.

column1: Message received: “Everyone else on your team enrolled in the new benefits portal last week — you’re the only one left.” Which tactic is the sender using?

Social pressure built on what everyone else has supposedly already done is consensus (EK 2.1.A.5). The message names no deadline, no limited supply, and no position of power — only the discomfort of being the last holdout.
(A) Incorrect — scarcity restricts a resource (“only three seats left”). Here the portal is open to the whole team
column2: what is limited is social cover, not supply.

column1: (C) Incorrect — urgency names a cutoff and a consequence for missing it. “Last week” describes the past and sets no deadline.
(D) Incorrect — authority requires the sender to hold or borrow power over the target. A comparison to peers carries no power.

Exam Tip: Consensus and urgency both push you to act now, for different reasons: consensus says everyone already did, urgency says time is running out. Underline the phrase carrying the pressure before you choose.
Incident report: a contractor holding valid VPN credentials copies design files and sells them after being passed over for a permanent role. Which adversary type is this?

Two facts decide it: legitimate credentials and access, plus a revenge motive. That is the insider adversary (EK 2.1.B.3). A contractor still counts — insiders are defined by the access they were granted, not by their job title.
(A) Incorrect — script kiddies run tools developed by others and do not start with authorized access to the target.
(B) Incorrect — a hacktivist acts to advance a cause. Selling the files for personal profit is not a cause.
(D) Incorrect — cyberterrorists target civil infrastructure to disrupt communities, regions, or nations, not one employer’s design files.
Exam Tip: Ask how the adversary got in before you ask why. Authorized access at the start of an incident points to an insider almost every time.
Incident report: a group deploys ransomware across a chain of hospitals and resells the stolen intellectual property in illegal markets, purely for money. Which adversary type is this?

Ransomware at scale plus resale of stolen intellectual property, with money given as the motive, is the transnational criminal organization (EK 2.1.B.5). Hospitals being the victim does not by itself make the attack terrorism.
(A) Incorrect — hacktivists pursue a cause, and “purely for money” rules a cause out.
(B) Incorrect — a coordinated multi-site ransomware and resale operation is beyond the capability of an adversary running someone else’s tools, and the motive named is revenue, not recognition.
(C) Incorrect — cyberterrorists are defined by political or ideological motive. The target fits
Exam Tip: On adversary-type items the motive sentence is the answer key. Two adversaries can hit the same target, so separate them by why rather than by what was hit.
One description below misstates its adversary type. Predict the error before you read the choices. Which description is wrong?

Cyberterrorists are defined by political or ideological motive and by targeting civil infrastructure (EK 2.1.B.4). They may act independently or on behalf of governments or criminal organizations, and skill level is no part of the definition. This option packs two errors into one sentence.
(A) Not the error — this is an accurate description of script kiddies (EK 2.1.B.1).
(B) Not the error — this is an accurate description of hacktivists (EK 2.1.B.2).
(D) Not the error — insiders can be recruited by outside parties, which is why access reviews matter (EK 2.1.B.3).
Exam Tip: On spot-the-error items the absolutes are where the error hides. Check every “always,” “never,” and “only” before you check anything else.

A club’s phishing-awareness poster pairs three sample messages with the tactic each one uses.
I. “Only three license seats are left for the free upgrade — claim yours before they run out.” — scarcity
II. “I’m calling from your bank’s fraud desk
column2:
I just need to verify the code we texted you.” — pretexting
III. “Your manager told me to have you reset the shared password today.” — consensus
Which pairings are correct?

column1: I is scarcity: a limited number of seats. II is pretexting: inventing a believable reason to make contact (EK 2.1.A.2). III is authority, not consensus — it borrows power from the target’s manager (EK 2.1.A.3). Consensus (EK 2.1.A.5) would have claimed that other people had already reset the password.
(A) Incorrect — I is right, but a caller inventing a fraud-desk identity is a textbook pretext, so II belongs in the answer.
(C) Incorrect — III is mislabeled. Nothing in it claims that anyone else has already complied.
(D) Incorrect — II is right, but III is authority rather than consensus, so the pair fails.

Exam Tip: Judge each roman-numeral statement true or false on its own and write the marks down. Then pick the choice that matches your marks exactly — do not let a familiar-looking pairing talk you out of them.

Exercise 1 — Physical Attacks and How Threats Exploit Them
6 questions — Name the attack, separate the vulnerability from the threat, and trace the compromise

column4: >Predict the answer before selecting an option

column1: Xtensr Research Labs has acquired a smaller research company across town, and you are on the physical security team running the assessment of the new building. This exercise works through the walkthrough notes: name each physical attack correctly, separate the vulnerability from the threat, and state the compromise that would follow.

A first-year analyst writes this finding for the assessment: “Employees at the new lab often chat with the front guard while badging in, so an adversary could stand behind them and enter unnoticed. This is card cloning, and the fix is to replace the badge readers with keypads.” Which statement identifies the errors in the finding?

There are two errors. The behavior described is tailgating (EK 2.2.A.3) — an adversary gains access by following close behind an authorized individual without that individual’s awareness. Card cloning (EK 2.2.A.6) is making a copy of an authorized user’s access card, which is not happening here. The recommended fix is also wrong: a keypad still authorizes one entry, and a distracted employee still lets a second person through. An access control vestibule or turnstile is the control that prevents one authorization from admitting two people (EK 2.3.B.5).
(A) Incorrect — the attack is misnamed, and keypads do nothing about a second person walking in on someone else’s authorization.
(B) Incorrect — shoulder surfing (EK 2.2.A.4) is watching a user access sensitive information so it can be used later
column2: nothing is observed and reused here.

column1: (D) Incorrect — dumpster diving (EK 2.2.A.5) is searching a target’s physical trash
column2: the finding involves no discarded material.

column1: Exam Tip: Re-derive the attack name from the behavior described, then check that the recommended control actually blocks that behavior. A wrong name almost always drags a wrong control with it.

Three incidents are logged at the new lab’s rear entrance. Decide your own answer first: which incidents are examples of piggybacking?
I. A person balancing two boxes of copier paper waits by the door until an employee opens it and holds it for them.
II. A person in a utility uniform tells an employee they need to inspect the sprinkler riser and is walked inside without a work order.
III. A person moves quickly and silently through the door as it swings shut behind a departing employee who never looks back.

Piggybacking is when an adversary uses social engineering to manipulate an authorized individual into granting access to a restricted area (EK 2.2.A.2), and the framework names these tactics directly: carrying something large so an authorized person holds the door, claiming to have forgotten an access token, and posing as maintenance staff who need to inspect or repair something. Incidents I and II are those two tactics. Incident III is tailgating (EK 2.2.A.3) — the departing employee never becomes aware, so nothing was granted.
(A) Incomplete — incident II is the maintenance-worker piggybacking tactic named in EK 2.2.A.2, so it belongs with incident I.
(C) Incorrect — incident III is tailgating rather than piggybacking, and incident I is a piggybacking tactic that this option leaves out.
(D) Incorrect — incident III involves no awareness or decision by the departing employee, which places it under tailgating.
Exam Tip: Every piggybacking tactic in the framework needs a human to say yes. If nobody in the story decides to help, you are looking at tailgating.

An adversary spends a week studying the new lab. Each observation below describes one of the physical attacks named in Topic 2.2 EXCEPT one. Which observation does not describe a Topic 2.2 physical attack?

<div class=""fb-exp"">Option A is shoulder surfing, including the camera variant EK 2.2.A.4 calls out. Option B is dumpster diving (EK 2.2.A.5). Option C is card cloning (EK 2.2.A.6) — copying an authorized user’s access card so the adversary inherits everything that user can reach. Option D is a pretexting attack delivered remotely: real, but a Topic 2.1 social engineering attack rather than a physical one. Social engineering often supports a physical attack (EK 2.2.A.1)
column2: the test is whether the adversary is acting on the physical space or on a physical object.

column1: (A) This is shoulder surfing — EK 2.2.A.4 explicitly includes recording the target with a camera for later analysis.
(B) This is dumpster diving — going through a target’s physical trash for information that advances the adversary’s goal.
(C) This is card cloning — producing a copy of an authorized user’s access card in order to use that user’s access.
Exam Tip: A Topic 2.2 attack requires the adversary to act on a physical space or a physical object. If the whole attack could run from another country, it belongs in Topic 2.1.

The new lab’s conference room holds a wall-mounted PC that stays logged into a shared scheduling account, and its USB ports are enabled and within reach. Which statement BEST explains why the assessor rates this a serious vulnerability rather than a minor inconvenience?

When adversaries gain physical access to a device and its ports, they can plug in a keylogger or an external drive containing malware, which can collect data from a user or possibly give the adversary control of the device (EK 2.2.B.5). That is a compromise of the device itself, not merely an information leak, and physical access to devices lets adversaries bypass many technical controls and layers of security (EK 2.2.C.1). Disabling USB ports is the matching control (EK 2.3.B.6).
(B) Incorrect — occupancy patterns are useful reconnaissance for an adversary, but they do not amount to device compromise.
(C) Incorrect — weak accountability is a real drawback of shared accounts, yet it does not explain the severity of reachable ports.
(D) Incorrect — license allocation is a cost question and does not belong in a vulnerability finding at all.
Exam Tip: For a physical finding, ask what the adversary can do with the access, not only what they can see. Port access escalates to control of the device, which outranks disclosure.

The assessment has to separate the vulnerability from the threat in every finding. For the finding “the loading-dock door latch is broken and the door rests unlatched overnight,” which pairing is correct?
<label class=""option-label""><input type=""radio"" name=""qq5"" value=""A""> <span>(A) The vulnerability is theft of the equipment inside
column2: the threat is the broken door latch

column1: <label class=""option-label""><input type=""radio"" name=""qq5"" value=""B""> <span>(B) The vulnerability is the overnight hours
column2: the threat is the loading dock sitting behind the building

column1: <label class=""option-label""><input type=""radio"" name=""qq5"" value=""C""> <span>(C) The vulnerability is the value of the equipment inside
column2: the threat is the missing camera on the dock

column1: <label class=""option-label""><input type=""radio"" name=""qq5"" value=""D""> <span>(D) The vulnerability is the broken door latch
column2: the threat is an adversary or event that could exploit it to enter and take or damage assets

column1: A vulnerability is a weakness or flaw that could allow an asset to be compromised (EK 2.2.B.2), which is the broken latch. A threat is what could act on that weakness — human adversaries seeking harm or disruption, and natural events as well (EK 2.2.B.1). Keeping the two apart is what lets you state the compromise cleanly: unauthorized access to a restricted physical space, followed by theft or destruction of resources.
(A) Incorrect — this reverses the pair. Theft is the compromise that results, and the latch is the weakness rather than the actor.
(B) Incorrect — the hours and the location both affect likelihood, but neither is the flaw itself nor the party acting on it.
(C) Incorrect — asset value drives impact, and a missing camera is a second vulnerability, not the threat.
Exam Tip: Vulnerability is the flaw. Threat is who or what acts on it. Compromise is what happens as a result. Mixing the three is the fastest way to lose points on a documented risk.

The new lab’s electrical box sits in an unlocked exterior alcove, and the badge readers, cameras, and specimen freezers all draw from it with no backup power. Which consequence should the assessment document as the MOST direct result of an adversary opening that box and pulling the main breaker?

When adversaries disrupt power to a device, the device and any services it provides become unavailable (EK 2.2.B.3), and damaging fuses or breakers is one of the named ways to do it. What makes this finding worse than a simple outage is that the detection and access controls run on the same power, so one physical act removes several layers at once. An uninterruptible power supply or a generator is the matching control (EK 2.3.B.7).
(A) Incorrect — cutting power does not make stored data readable
column2: this confuses an availability compromise with a confidentiality one.

column1: (B) Incorrect — modifying the reader database is an unauthorized-modification compromise and requires access to the system, not to the breaker.
(D) Incorrect — an outage stops new footage from being recorded
column2: it does not hand the adversary the footage already stored.

column1: Exam Tip: Power findings map to availability. Name the compromise the framework names — the device and its services become unavailable — then check which other controls share that power source.

6 questions — Choose the managerial and physical controls that answer each walkthrough finding

column4: >Predict the answer before selecting an option

column1: Xtensr Research Labs — Delmar Applied Optics

You are on the physical security team at Xtensr Research Labs. Xtensr is acquiring Delmar Applied Optics, a smaller research company in the same town, and your walkthrough of the Delmar building is finished. The findings are on record: a finished-lens vault, an engineering file server on a shelf in an unlocked utility closet, a reception PC on the internal wireless network with exposed USB ports, a badge controller cabinet standing unlocked in the open lobby, a testing bay fed by a single power panel, and a ground-floor optics bay below street grade on a floodplain. Assessing the risk was the last exercise. This one is the recommendation: which control answers which finding, and what gets funded first.

<div class=""q-stem"">Xtensr is drafting a security awareness training module for the Delmar staff who will stay on after the acquisition. Four objectives are proposed. Three of them describe employee behavior that awareness training exists to change
column2: one describes an administrative duty instead, and does not belong in this module. Which objective does NOT belong?

column1: Security awareness training is a managerial control aimed squarely at what employees do: detect social engineering such as phishing, refuse to badge other people into restricted areas, and prevent device theft. Options (A), (B) and (D) are those three behaviors written for the Delmar building. Option (C) is a records-retention and audit duty owned by the compliance function — no amount of training an ordinary employee changes how long a log is kept or who reviews it.
(A) Incorrect — recognizing a social engineering attempt and reporting instead of replying is the phishing objective this module is built around.
(B) Incorrect — refusing to badge another person into a restricted area is the training objective that answers the tailgating finding at the engineering wing door.
(D) Incorrect — preventing device theft, including cabling a laptop and putting portable media away, is trained employee behavior.

Exam Tip: Test a training objective by asking whether an employee could meet it by changing what they personally do. If the objective is really about a policy being written, a log being kept, or a system being configured, it belongs somewhere other than awareness training.

Delmar has no workstation security policy at all. Xtensr must write one, tiered by the sensitivity of the data handled at each workstation: the reception PC records walk-in visitors, while the engineering workstations hold lens design files. Three measures are proposed.

I. Fit the reception PC with a privacy screen filter so a person standing at the counter cannot read the display.
II. Connect the engineering workstations to an uninterruptible power supply so an outage does not interrupt work in progress.
III. Install a turnstile at the engineering wing entrance so each person entering must authenticate individually.

Which measures belong in the workstation security policy itself?

A workstation security policy sets out the measures that protect a workstation, and it may carry tiers based on the type of data handled there. A privacy screen filter (I) and connecting devices to surge protectors or an uninterruptible power supply (II) are both written into that policy — the UPS is the measure students most often leave out, because it protects availability while the rest of the policy reads as confidentiality. A turnstile (III) is a physical control at a building entry point: it protects the wing, not the workstation, so it is recommended separately.
(A) Incomplete — a workstation security policy also covers connecting the device to a surge protector or an uninterruptible power supply, which is measure II.
(C) Incorrect — the turnstile guards an entrance rather than a desk, and this option drops the privacy screen filter, which is a standard workstation measure.
(D) Incorrect — two of the three belong in the policy, but a turnstile at the wing entrance is a separate physical control on the building and is not a workstation measure.

Exam Tip: A workstation security policy covers locking the device before leaving it unattended, clearing sensitive documents from the desk, privacy screens, and surge protectors or a UPS. If a measure protects a room or a doorway instead of a desk, it is a different control on a different line of the report.

Delmar’s engineering file server sits on a shelf in an unlocked utility closet, off a corridor that any badged Delmar employee may walk down. Xtensr recommends a keyed lock on the closet door and a locking cabinet around the server itself. A Delmar manager objects: “A lock on that closet is pointless — everyone who can reach that corridor has already badged into the building.” Which response is BEST?

Locks on doors, server cabinets, and computers exist to prevent a device from being accessed or stolen, and they do it by narrowing who can physically reach it. The badge reader is one layer and it admits every employee. The closet lock is a further layer and it admits only key holders. The cabinet lock is a third. The manager’s objection would hold only if the two layers admitted the same population — and they do not, which is the entire point of putting one behind the other.
(A) Incorrect — a camera records an entry after it has happened
column2: it does not stop the server being reached. Swapping a preventative control for a detective one leaves the access itself unaddressed.

column1: (B) Incorrect — an instruction to stay out of the closet asks for cooperation from precisely the person who would ignore it. A lock does not depend on the adversary agreeing to it.

(C) Incorrect — the conclusion is right and the justification is invented. No such success rate was measured here, and reaching a correct verdict from a number nobody produced is the habit these questions are written to break.
Exam Tip: Judge layered controls by who each layer admits, not by how many layers you can count. A second control that admits the same population as the first adds nothing
column2: one that admits fewer people adds a real layer.

column1: Delmar’s ground-floor optics bay fronts a street where delivery vehicles reverse up to the curb, and the bay’s glass frontage sits directly behind them. Xtensr recommends a line of bollards along that frontage. Which statement BEST describes what that recommendation accomplishes?

Fencing, gates, and bollards are perimeter controls. They deter an adversary from trying to physically access a building, and they obstruct a vehicle that tries anyway. That is the whole of what they do: they check no identity, they record nothing, and they are not a flood control. Naming a control’s function precisely is what lets you tell whether it actually answers the finding you raised.
(B) Incorrect — authentication is what a card reader does. A bollard cannot tell one person from another
column2: it obstructs everyone in exactly the same way.

column1: (C) Incorrect — detection is what a camera, a motion sensor, or a guard does. A bollard raises no alert and produces no feed for anyone to monitor.
(D) Incorrect — the optics bay floods because it sits below street grade on a floodplain, and bollards are spaced posts rather than a barrier. That finding needs its own mitigation.

Exam Tip: Sort a physical control by function before you defend it. Preventative controls stop the attack, detective controls reveal it, corrective controls restore what it damaged. Bollards, locks and vestibules are preventative
column2: cameras, motion sensors and guards are detective.

column1:
Xtensr’s draft report maps each Delmar finding to a recommended control. Exactly one row recommends a control that does not act on the compromise its finding creates.

1. A stranger followed a technician through the engineering wing door → install an access control vestibule at that entrance
2. The reception PC has exposed USB ports in an area anyone may walk into → disable the USB ports on that PC
3. A Delmar badge was photographed on a lanyard in the open lobby, and the badge controller cabinet stands unlocked beside it → connect the badge controller to an uninterruptible power supply
4. The engineering file server sits in an unlocked utility closet → fit a keyed lock on the closet and a locking cabinet on the server

Which correction is BEST?

Choosing a relevant control means asking how an adversary would exploit the vulnerability, then checking that the control prevents, detects, or corrects that specific thing. Rows 1, 2 and 4 all do it: a vestibule stops a second person passing on one authentication, disabling the ports stops a drive being loaded, and locks stop the server being reached. Row 3’s finding is a photographed badge beside an unlocked controller cabinet, so the compromise is unauthorized access — to a credential, and to the equipment that issues credentials. An uninterruptible power supply answers a power outage, which is not what happened in that lobby.

(A) Incorrect — training is worth adding, but a technician cannot watch a door he has already walked away from. A vestibule admits one authenticated person at a time whether or not anybody is paying attention, so row 1 was already sound.
(B) Incorrect — a cabinet lock protects the inside of the machine, while the exposed ports are on the outside and stay usable. Row 2’s port lockout already acts on the compromise.

(C) Incorrect — and this is the tempting one, because it is a genuine improvement to a row that was not broken: the keyed lock already prevents the access, and a card reader would add a record of it. The question asks which row recommends a control that does not act on its compromise, and row 4’s does.

Exam Tip: Read every recommendation as a claim about one specific compromise. Say the compromise out loud — unauthorized access to data or restricted space, disruption of services, theft or destruction of resources, unauthorized modification of data — then confirm the control acts on that one. The row to correct is the row that answers a different compromise.
<div class=""q-stem"">Xtensr’s Delmar remediation budget will cover only two recommendations this quarter
column2:
the rest wait for next year’s cycle. The four candidates carry these assessments.

W. Keyed lock and locking cabinet for the engineering file server — high severity, low cost
X. Access control vestibule at the engineering wing entrance — high severity, high cost
Y. Disabling the USB ports on the reception PC — moderate severity, negligible cost
Z. Bollards around the full building perimeter — low severity, high cost

Which pair should Xtensr fund first?

column1: Organizations prioritize mitigations on two axes at once: how severe the risk is, and what the mitigation costs. W is high severity at low cost and Y is moderate severity at essentially no cost, so together they retire more risk per dollar than any other pair and leave most of the quarter’s budget intact. X is a sound recommendation and will be funded, but it is an expensive way to spend one quarter. Z is lowest on severity and highest on cost, which puts it last by both measures.
(A) Incorrect — funding from the top of the price list down retires the least risk per dollar. Cost is a reason to sequence a mitigation, never a reason to promote it.
(C) Incorrect — severity on its own would buy X ahead of Y, but the framework weighs severity against cost. Y costs almost nothing and its risk is real
column2: deferring it to afford one expensive control is a poor trade.

column1: (D) Incorrect — Y does belong in the funded pair, but on severity and cost rather than on position. Z is the lowest severity and the highest cost of the four, and “outer layers first” is not how mitigations are ranked.
Exam Tip: When a question hands you severity and cost together, it is testing whether you weigh them together. High severity at low cost is the first thing funded
column2: low severity at high cost is the last. A tie on severity is broken by cost.

Scored six-question MCQ exercise on CED Topic 2.4 — how controls detect physical attacks and where to put them — for AP Cybersecurity."",""author"":{""@type"":""Person"",""name"":""Tanner Crow"",""url"":""https://www.apcsexamprep.com/pages/ap-computer-science-tutor""},""publisher"":{""@type"":""Organization"",""name"":""APCSExamPrep.com"",""url"":""https://www.apcsexamprep.com""},""educationalLevel"":""High School"",""inLanguage"":""en-US""},
6 questions — Decide what watches Delmar, and where it goes

column4: >Predict the answer before selecting an option

column1: Xtensr Research Labs has closed on Delmar Applied Optics. The risk assessment is finished and the $150,000 control plan from the last exercise is funded and installed: a card reader, door contact and access control vestibule at the finished-lens vault
column2: a locked enclosure with a tamper switch around the lobby badge controller
column3: the engineering file server relocated out of the unlocked utility closet into a locked cabinet
column4: port blockers and a privacy screen on the reception PC
column5: a UPS in the testing bay
column6: flood barriers and raised racking in the below-grade optics bay. Prevention is bought. Your job now is monitoring — deciding what would detect an attack on this building, and where each control has to sit to do it.

column1: Delmar’s installer submits this note for the corridor camera outside the finished-lens vault: “Mount at 5 ft on the corridor wall, about 20 ft back from the vault door and angled at it, on a hand-adjustable swivel bracket so the lens can be re-aimed during cleaning.” Which statement identifies the most serious weakness in this placement?

EK 2.4.B.1 asks you to weigh three things for a camera: visual coverage, angle, and tamper resistance. The first two are fine here. The third fails: a camera an adversary can reach on the way past is a camera the adversary controls, and the careful angle survives only as long as nobody turns the bracket. Mount it out of reach and fix the bracket, and the same placement works.
(A) Incorrect — the distance and angle are defensible. What fails is tamper resistance, the third thing 2.4.B.1 tells you to weigh and the easiest to skip.
(B) Incorrect — trays in frame show what was taken, not who took it. The door-facing angle is the right call
column2: it just has to survive contact with the adversary.

column1: (C) Incorrect — this is true, and it is still true after the mount is fixed, so it is not the weakness this note introduces. Badge attribution comes from the reader’s log, not from the camera.

Exam Tip: Run all three parts of 2.4.B.1 in order — coverage, angle, tamper resistance — and stop at the first one that fails. A statement can be perfectly true about a camera and still not be the flaw in its placement.

The funded plan puts an access control vestibule at the finished-lens vault entry, alongside the card reader and door contact. Consider three claims about what the vestibule contributes to detecting physical attacks:

  I. It stops a second person from entering on one badge presentation, whether or not the badge holder agreed to it.
  II. It makes each vault entry attributable to a single badge, so the door log narrows down who was inside during the window a lens went missing.
  III. It removes the need to monitor the corridor camera, because no unauthorized person can reach the vault door.

Which claims are correct?

The vestibule does both jobs. It defeats piggybacking and tailgating — the consented and the uninvited follower alike (2.3.B.3) — and because exactly one badge opens exactly one entry, it turns the door log into evidence an investigator can actually use, which is the after-incident value 2.4.A.1 attaches to recordings. III overreaches: a vestibule governs one doorway, not the corridor, and it produces no record at all of someone who never presents a badge.
(A) Incorrect — I is right, but so is II. The one-badge-one-entry attribution is exactly what makes an entry log worth reading after an incident.
(B) Incorrect — II is right, but I is not wrong. Stopping an uninvited follower and stopping a consenting one are both inside what a vestibule does.
(D) Incorrect — and internally inconsistent. If no unauthorized person could reach the vault door, there would be nothing for the log in II to narrow down.

Exam Tip: A preventive control can still be a detection asset — locks, readers and vestibules all generate logs. What none of them ever do is remove the need for a layer watching what they do not control.
Delmar can fund one security officer for the overnight shift. The vault already has a card reader, door contact, vestibule and an interior motion sensor
column2: the lobby badge-controller cabinet has a locked enclosure and a tamper switch
column3: the ground-floor optics bay sits below street grade with exterior windows at sidewalk level and no funded monitoring. Which assignment makes the best use of the single officer?

column1: <div class=""fb-exp"">EK 2.4.B.4: stationary guards suit funnels and single high-value items
column2: patrolling guards suit perimeters and exterior areas. The vault is already the most instrumented point in this building — four layers watch that one door. The exterior and the below-grade bay have nothing. Guard placement is a coverage decision, so the officer goes where the hardware is not.

column1: (A) Incorrect — a stationary post is the right form for one concentrated high-value item, but four controls already watch that door, so the officer adds less there than anywhere else.
(C) Incorrect — the tamper switch already reports any attempt on that cabinet, and a finding’s severity ranking is not what decides guard placement. Coverage gaps are.

(D) Incorrect — this re-covers the most instrumented space in the building. A patrol’s value is the time pressure it puts on an adversary, and a fixed published interval over ground that sensors already hold turns that pressure into a timetable.

Exam Tip: Guards are placed against gaps, not against asset value. Find the asset no control is watching, then match the form to the ground: stationary where traffic funnels or value concentrates, patrolling for perimeters and exterior areas.

Delmar’s corridor and lobby cameras record to a unit that overwrites the oldest footage after 72 hours. Finished lenses are counted once a month, and a shortage found in the March count is the first sign anything was taken. Which change would do the most to make the camera system useful to that investigation?

EK 2.4.A.1 says recordings are especially valuable after an incident — but only footage that still exists. A 72-hour window against a 30-day detection interval guarantees the relevant recording is gone before anyone knows to look for it. Retention has to be matched to how long this organization takes to notice, not to how long the disk holds out.
(B) Incorrect — more cameras produce more footage that is overwritten on the same 72-hour clock. Coverage is not the binding constraint in this stem.
(C) Incorrect — resolution improves footage you still have, and 30 days after the theft there is none of it left to improve.
(D) Incorrect — monitoring a feed is genuinely valuable and it is the right answer to a different question. A shortage discovered at a monthly count was not visible to a watcher weeks earlier.

Exam Tip: When a stem hands you two time spans — how long footage is kept, and how long the organization takes to notice — compare them before anything else. A detection control that expires before detection happens contributes nothing.

One row of Delmar’s draft monitoring plan is below. Exactly one field is wrong.

  Asset: engineering file server, locked cabinet in the utility closet
  Detection control: door contact on the closet door, reporting to the badge system
  Alert goes to: the overnight monitoring service
  Expected response: an officer checks the closet on the next scheduled patrol pass
  Retention: contact events kept 90 days

Which correction fixes the field that is actually wrong?

A sensor is worth exactly the response it triggers (EK 2.4.A.2, 2.4.A.3). Everything else in this row holds up: a contact is a legitimate detection control for a door that should stay shut, an off-site service is staffed precisely when the building is not, and 90 days comfortably outlasts any interval in which a missing server would go unnoticed. The defect is that the response is scheduled instead of immediate — the alert arrives in time to matter and then waits.
(A) Incorrect — a contact and a camera answer different questions, and this is a detection row, not an identification row. The contact does the job the row claims for it.
(B) Incorrect — that corridor is unstaffed overnight, which is exactly when an unobserved closet entry is likeliest. Routing to a staffed service is the stronger choice, not the flaw.
(C) Incorrect — 90 days already outruns the interval in which anyone would notice the server missing, so retention is not the field that fails here.

Exam Tip: On a “one field is wrong” item, do not stop at the first field you could improve — three options will improve something that was already adequate. Ask which field, left exactly as written, still lets the attack succeed.

The vault’s interior motion sensor is installed and armed overnight. As configured, an activation sends an email to the facilities shared inbox, which is read when the office opens. The building is unstaffed from 7 p.m. to 7 a.m. Which change does the most to make this sensor a working detection control rather than a record?
<div class=""fb-exp"">EK 2.4.A.3 has the sensor alert security to movement
column2: EK 2.4.A.2 has security respond once activity is detected. The two are a pair, and this configuration only does the first half. An alert sitting in an inbox for twelve hours is an after-incident record — useful, but not detection in the sense the CED means. Send it to someone awake and able to act and the loop closes.

column1: (A) Incorrect — sensitivity governs whether movement registers, not whether anyone acts on it. In a low-traffic vault it mainly buys the false alarms 2.4.B.2 warns about.
(C) Incorrect — a second sensor addresses coverage, which the stem never says is failing, and its activations land in the same unread inbox.
(D) Incorrect — an audible alarm deters, and it may shorten the intrusion, but it dispatches nobody. A warned intruder in an unstaffed building still leaves unchallenged.
Exam Tip: Trace every alert to a named person and a time of day. If the answer is “a shared inbox, in the morning,” the control documents attacks

6 questions — Evaluate network architecture and attack surface concepts

column4: >Predict the answer before selecting an option

column1: Brightpath University operates a campus network serving 15,000 students, 2,000 faculty, and 500 administrative staff. The network includes student Wi-Fi, faculty workstations, research lab servers, a student information system (SIS), and IoT devices (smart boards, security cameras, HVAC). The IT security team is conducting a network architecture review.

Brightpath’s IT team inventories the campus network: 3,000 student laptops on Wi-Fi, 800 faculty workstations, 45 servers, 200 IoT devices, a VPN gateway, 12 web applications, and a guest Wi-Fi portal. Which statement BEST describes the university’s attack surface?

Attack surface = every potential entry/exit point. For Brightpath: 4,000+ endpoints, 45 servers, 200 IoT devices, VPN, 12 web apps, guest Wi-Fi, user accounts, APIs. Reducing attack surface means minimizing unnecessary exposure.
(A) The VPN is one entry point
column2: the attack surface includes every device and service.

column1: (C) License count is an inventory metric, not an attack surface measure.
(D) Physical campus size does not determine network attack surface.
Exam Tip: Attack surface = everything an attacker could target. Larger organizations have larger surfaces. Reducing it means disabling unused services, closing ports, and segmenting access.

A Brightpath network engineer troubleshoots connectivity between a student laptop and the SIS server. The issue is that the laptop can reach the server’s IP address (ping works) but cannot load the web application (HTTPS fails). At which OSI layer is the problem MOST likely occurring?

Ping (ICMP) works at Layer 3, proving IP routing is functional. Layers 1-3 are working. The failure at HTTPS (Layer 7) points to the web server configuration, TLS certificate, or application-level issue.
(A) If the cable were damaged, ping would also fail.
(B) If routing were broken, ping would not reach the server.
(D) If the switch port were misconfigured, no traffic would flow at all.
Exam Tip: Troubleshooting with OSI: if lower layers work (ping succeeds = L1-3 OK), the problem is at a higher layer. HTTPS failure with working ping = Layer 7 issue.
Brightpath’s video lecture streaming platform uses UDP for live video delivery but TCP for the student login portal. Which of the following BEST explains this design choice?

TCP provides reliable, ordered delivery with error correction — critical for authentication where every byte matters. UDP sacrifices reliability for speed — acceptable for video streaming where a dropped frame is invisible to viewers.
(A) UDP is not inherently more secure
(D) Reversed — TCP is more reliable but slower
Exam Tip: TCP = reliable, ordered (web, SSH, email, login). UDP = fast, no guarantee (video, DNS, VoIP, gaming). Choose by whether the application tolerates data loss.

A security scan reveals that a Brightpath research server has 47 open ports. The server only needs ports 443 (HTTPS management), 22 (SSH administration), and 3306 (MySQL database). What should the IT team do with the remaining 44 ports?
<div class=""fb-exp"">Every open port is an attack surface entry point. Closing unnecessary ports is one of the most effective hardening measures. The server needs 3 ports
column2: the other 44 offer zero value and 44 additional risks.

column1: (A) Keeping ports open “just in case” is a security anti-pattern.
(B) Security through obscurity (renaming ports) is easily defeated by scanning tools.
(D) Opening more ports on more servers increases total attack surface.
Exam Tip: Port hardening: identify needed services, close everything else. Nmap can discover non-standard port numbers in seconds, so renaming provides no real protection.
<div class=""q-stem"">A phishing attack targets Brightpath by compromising the campus DNS server. The attacker modifies the DNS record for <code style=""background:#EDE9FE!important
column5: >portal.brightpath.edu to point to the attacker’s server instead of the real SIS. Students who type the correct URL are redirected to a fake login page. Which statement is CORRECT?

column1: DNS spoofing is dangerous precisely because the URL looks correct. The browser resolves the domain to whatever IP the DNS server provides. Without DNSSEC or certificate validation, the student sees the correct URL pointing to the wrong server.
(A) DNS cache poisoning and server compromise are well-documented attack vectors.
(B) The URL is correct — DNS changes the IP behind it, not the domain name.
(D) The attack works with the correct URL
column2: that is what makes it effective.

column1: Exam Tip: DNS spoofing = correct URL, wrong server. Defenses: DNSSEC (cryptographic verification of DNS responses) and HTTPS certificate validation (the fake server cannot present a valid cert for brightpath.edu).

Brightpath’s network diagram shows the campus firewall connected to the internet, a DMZ containing the public web server, an internal network with VLANs for students/faculty/admin, and a separate SCADA network for building automation. Which of the following is NOT a valid reason for documenting this topology?

Publishing network topology publicly gives attackers a roadmap of the infrastructure. Topology documentation is an internal security tool — it helps defenders plan, but it must be protected as sensitive information.
(A) Valid — topology diagrams reveal attack paths for defensive analysis.
(B) Valid — incident response requires understanding network connectivity.
(D) Valid — topology maps reveal single points of failure and segmentation gaps.
Exam Tip: Network topology = sensitive internal documentation. It helps defenders plan and attackers navigate. Never publish externally. Restrict access to IT and security teams.

Scored MCQ exercise covering DDoS, ARP poisoning, DNS spoofing, and session hijacking for AP Cyber."",""author"":{""@type"":""Person"",""name"":""Tanner Crow"",""url"":""https://www.apcsexamprep.com/pages/ap-computer-science-tutor""},""publisher"":{""@type"":""Organization"",""name"":""APCSExamPrep.com"",""url"":""https://www.apcsexamprep.com""},""educationalLevel"":""High School"",""inLanguage"":""en-US""},
6 questions — Identify attack types from network incident descriptions

column4: >Predict the attack type before selecting an option

column1: Harborview Regional Bank operates 12 branches across the Pacific Northwest, serving 45,000 customers. The bank runs a centralized data center with customer-facing online banking, internal teller systems, and a SWIFT terminal for international transfers. The security operations center (SOC) has flagged six network anomalies in the past 48 hours.

Harborview’s online banking portal is receiving 4.2 million HTTP requests per second from 92,000 unique IP addresses spanning 40 countries. Legitimate customers cannot access their accounts. The traffic pattern shows randomized User-Agent strings and no repeated payloads. Which attack type is MOST likely occurring?

The massive volume (4.2M req/sec), global distribution (92K IPs, 40 countries), and randomized patterns are hallmarks of a botnet-driven DDoS attack. The geographic spread rules out a single-source flood.
(A) Incorrect — SYN floods target the TCP handshake, not HTTP layer traffic. The description specifies HTTP requests.
(C) Incorrect — DNS amplification uses UDP, not HTTP requests, and targets bandwidth rather than application layer.
(D) Incorrect — ARP poisoning operates on the local LAN segment, not from 92,000 external IPs.
Exam Tip: DDoS = distributed (many sources). DoS = single source. The number of unique IPs is the key differentiator in the scenario.
<div class=""q-stem"">A network analyst discovers that all traffic from teller workstations in Branch 7 is routing through an unknown device (MAC: <code style=""background:#EDE9FE!important
column5: >DE:AD:BE:EF:00:01) before reaching the default gateway. The ARP tables on affected workstations show this MAC address mapped to the gateway’s IP. Which of the following BEST describes this attack?

column1: The ARP tables explicitly show the attacker’s MAC mapped to the gateway IP — this is the defining signature of ARP poisoning. The attacker intercepts traffic destined for the gateway, establishing a man-in-the-middle position.
(A) Incorrect — DNS poisoning alters domain-to-IP mappings, not MAC-to-IP mappings in ARP tables.
(B) Incorrect — passive sniffing does not alter ARP tables
(D) Incorrect — VLAN hopping exploits switch trunk ports
column2: the evidence points specifically to ARP table corruption.

column1: Exam Tip: ARP maps IP addresses to MAC addresses on a local network. If the ARP table shows an unexpected MAC for the gateway, that is ARP poisoning.

column5:
>harborviewbank.com in their browser takes them to a page that looks identical to the real site but has a slightly different URL in the address bar. The fake site has a valid TLS certificate. Which of the following statements about this attack are correct?

I. The attacker likely poisoned a DNS resolver’s cache to return a malicious IP for harborviewbank.com.
II. The presence of a valid TLS certificate (padlock icon) guarantees that the site is operated by Harborview Bank.
III. Customers who verify the URL in their address bar before entering credentials would avoid this attack.

column1: <div class=""fb-exp"">Statement I is correct — DNS cache poisoning redirects the domain to a malicious IP. Statement II is incorrect — TLS certificates only verify that the connection is encrypted to the domain listed in the certificate
column2: an attacker can obtain a valid certificate for a similar-looking domain. Statement III is correct — checking the actual URL would reveal the domain mismatch.

column1: (A) Incomplete — Statement III is also correct.

column2: TLS does not guarantee site legitimacy.

column1: Exam Tip: HTTPS = encrypted connection. It does NOT mean the site is trustworthy. Attackers can and do obtain valid TLS certificates for phishing domains.

A security audit reveals that Harborview’s guest Wi-Fi segment and the internal teller network share the same physical switch without VLAN segmentation. An attacker on the guest network has placed their wireless adapter in promiscuous mode. Which type of data is the attacker LEAST likely to capture?

HTTPS encrypts the payload between the browser and the server using TLS. Even if the attacker captures these packets, the content (including session tokens) is encrypted and unreadable without the TLS keys. Options A, B, and D all involve unencrypted protocols where data is transmitted in plaintext.
(A) Likely captured — HTTP transmits credentials in plaintext, fully visible to a sniffer.
(B) Likely captured — unencrypted SMTP sends email content as readable text.
(D) Likely captured — standard DNS queries are unencrypted and reveal browsing patterns.
Exam Tip: Encryption is the primary defense against packet sniffing. HTTPS protects web traffic
column2: unencrypted protocols (HTTP, Telnet, FTP, basic SMTP) are fully exposed.

column1: An employee logs into the bank’s HR portal over an unencrypted connection. An attacker on the same network segment captures the session cookie and uses it from a different device to access the employee’s HR account. This attack is BEST classified as:

The attacker captured an existing valid session cookie from network traffic and replayed it — this is the textbook definition of session hijacking. The attack bypasses authentication entirely because the token represents an already-authenticated session.

column2: the attacker captured an active session token.

column1: (B) Incorrect — XSS involves injecting scripts into a web page
column2: the cookie was captured from network traffic.

column1: (D) Incorrect — SQL injection targets database queries
Exam Tip: Session hijacking = stealing an active session token. The attacker never needs the password. This is why session cookies must only be transmitted over HTTPS.

Harborview’s web server begins sending SYN/ACK packets to thousands of IP addresses that never initiated a connection. External organizations are reporting Harborview’s IP as a source of unwanted traffic. The bank’s IP is being added to blocklists. Which of the following BEST explains what is happening?

This is a SYN reflection/amplification attack. The attacker sends SYN packets to Harborview with the victim’s IP spoofed as the source address. Harborview’s server responds with SYN/ACK packets to the spoofed (victim) IPs. Harborview becomes an unwitting amplifier, and its IP gets blocklisted for sending unsolicited traffic.
(A) Incorrect — a compromised bot would send various attack traffic, not specifically SYN/ACK responses to addresses that never sent SYN packets.
(C) Incorrect — firewalls do not forward traffic back to senders as a misconfiguration pattern.
(D) Incorrect — port scanning sends SYN packets, not SYN/ACK packets
column2: the traffic pattern is responses, not initiations.

column1: Exam Tip: SYN reflection exploits the TCP handshake. The victim receives unsolicited SYN/ACK packets. The key clue: the server is sending responses to addresses that never initiated connections.

Scored MCQ exercise covering TLS, HTTPS, SSH, VPN, and certificate validation for AP Cyber."",""author"":{""@type"":""Person"",""name"":""Tanner Crow"",""url"":""https://www.apcsexamprep.com/pages/ap-computer-science-tutor""},""publisher"":{""@type"":""Organization"",""name"":""APCSExamPrep.com"",""url"":""https://www.apcsexamprep.com""},""educationalLevel"":""High School"",""inLanguage"":""en-US""},
6 questions — Evaluate protocol choices and encryption implementations

column4: >Predict the answer before selecting an option

column1: Brightpath University is upgrading its network infrastructure to eliminate insecure protocols. The IT security team has audited all network services and found that several departments still use legacy protocols that transmit data in plaintext. You are reviewing six protocol decisions and recommending secure alternatives.

Brightpath’s student portal currently runs on HTTP (port 80). Students log in with their university credentials to view grades, register for classes, and pay tuition. The IT team proposes migrating to HTTPS (port 443). Which of the following BEST describes what HTTPS adds that HTTP does not provide?

HTTPS wraps HTTP inside a TLS (Transport Layer Security) tunnel. This encrypts all data exchanged between the browser and server — including login credentials, grade data, and payment information — making it unreadable to anyone who intercepts the traffic.
(A) Incorrect — HTTPS does not replace authentication
column2: students still need credentials. HTTPS protects those credentials in transit.

column1: (C) Incorrect — HTTPS provides encryption, not compression. HTTP/2 includes compression features, but that is independent of TLS.
(D) Incorrect — HTTPS encrypts the transport layer
column2: it does not perform malware scanning on file content.

column1: Exam Tip: HTTP = plaintext. HTTPS = HTTP + TLS encryption. The “S” stands for Secure, meaning the transport is encrypted. It does not replace authentication or scan content.

The Computer Science department uses Telnet (port 23) to remotely manage Linux lab servers. A security audit flags this as a critical vulnerability. Which of the following statements about this risk are correct?

I. Telnet transmits all data, including passwords, in plaintext that can be captured by anyone on the network path.
II. SSH (port 22) provides the same remote terminal functionality as Telnet but encrypts the entire session.
III. Replacing Telnet with SSH requires replacing all the Linux servers with newer hardware.

<div class=""fb-exp"">Statement I is correct — Telnet sends everything, including authentication credentials, as readable plaintext. Statement II is correct — SSH provides encrypted remote terminal access with the same functionality. Statement III is incorrect — SSH is a software protocol that runs on existing hardware
(A) Incomplete — Statement II is also correct.
(C) Incorrect — includes the false Statement III.

column2: SSH is a software upgrade, not a hardware requirement.

column1: Exam Tip: Insecure → Secure replacements: Telnet → SSH, FTP → SFTP/FTPS, HTTP → HTTPS. The secure version encrypts the same functionality.

A student visiting the Brightpath library website sees a browser warning: “Your connection is not private — the certificate for library.brightpath.edu has expired.” The student clicks “Proceed anyway.” Which risk does this action introduce?

An expired certificate means the browser cannot verify that the server is who it claims to be. The TLS encryption may still function, but without a valid certificate, a man-in-the-middle attacker could present their own certificate and intercept all traffic. Clicking “Proceed anyway” bypasses this critical verification step.
(A) Incorrect — certificate expiration does not affect server data
(B) Incorrect — expired certificates do not disable browser security or trigger automatic downloads.
(D) Incorrect — certificate status has no effect on device visibility on the network.
Exam Tip: Certificate warnings mean the identity verification chain is broken. Encryption may still work, but you cannot be sure WHO you are encrypting to. This is exactly how MitM attacks succeed.

The Admissions Office transfers applicant files to a partner institution using FTP (port 21). The files contain Social Security numbers, transcripts, and financial aid data. The partner suggests switching to SFTP. Which of the following is NOT a valid reason to make this switch?

SFTP does NOT transfer files faster due to encryption. In fact, encryption adds computational overhead that can slightly reduce throughput. SFTP’s benefit is security (encryption), not performance. Options A, B, and D are all valid reasons to switch from FTP to SFTP.
(A) Valid reason — FTP plaintext transmission of SSNs is a critical vulnerability.
(B) Valid reason — SFTP encrypts the entire session using SSH.
(D) Valid reason — FERPA requires protection of student educational records, including during transmission.
Exam Tip: Encryption adds security but also adds processing overhead. It never makes transfers faster. If an answer claims encryption improves speed, it is incorrect.

Brightpath offers VPN access for faculty working remotely. The IT team is choosing between two configurations: (1) split-tunnel VPN that only routes university-bound traffic through the encrypted tunnel, or (2) full-tunnel VPN that routes ALL traffic through the university network. Which of the following BEST describes a security advantage of full-tunnel over split-tunnel?

Full-tunnel VPN forces ALL traffic — including personal web browsing, email, and cloud services — through the university’s network perimeter. This means the university’s firewall, IDS, and content filters inspect everything, providing the same protection as being on campus. Split-tunnel only protects university-bound traffic.
(A) Incorrect — full-tunnel does not encrypt faster
column2: it actually increases bandwidth load on the VPN concentrator.

column1: (C) Incorrect — perimeter security does not replace endpoint protection
(D) Incorrect — geographic content access is a side effect, not a security advantage.
Exam Tip: Split-tunnel = faster (less VPN bandwidth) but less secure. Full-tunnel = more secure (all traffic inspected) but higher bandwidth cost. The tradeoff is security vs. performance.

Brightpath’s DNS queries are currently sent in plaintext over UDP port 53. A network administrator proposes implementing DNS over HTTPS (DoH). Which of the following is a LEGITIMATE concern about deploying DoH on the campus network?

DoH encrypts DNS queries inside HTTPS, which protects student privacy but also blinds the university’s DNS-based security tools. Content filters, malware domain blocklists, and DNS monitoring all rely on reading DNS queries — DoH makes this traffic opaque. This is a real tradeoff between privacy and institutional security visibility.
(B) Incorrect — DoH is supported natively by Chrome, Firefox, Edge, and Safari.

column2: it just encrypts the query transport.

column1: (D) Incorrect — DoH encrypts DNS inside HTTPS
Exam Tip: Encryption is a double-edged sword: it protects privacy but can blind security monitoring. DoH is a real-world example of this tension between privacy and security visibility.

6 questions — Evaluate VLAN designs and segmentation policies

column4: >Predict the answer before selecting an option

column1: Sycamore School District serves 5,000 students across 8 schools. The district network includes student Chromebook traffic, teacher workstations with access to the student information system (SIS), administrative offices handling payroll, a guest Wi-Fi network for visitors, and IoT devices (security cameras, HVAC controllers). All traffic currently flows through a single flat network with no segmentation.

Sycamore’s entire district operates on a single flat network (10.0.0.0/16) with no VLANs. A student connects a personal device to a classroom Ethernet port and runs a network scanner. Which of the following systems could the student’s device potentially discover and attempt to access?

On a flat network with no segmentation, all devices share a single broadcast domain. A scanner can discover and attempt to reach every connected device — student laptops, administrative servers, IoT cameras, payroll systems — because no logical boundaries exist between network zones.
(A) Incorrect — switches forward traffic based on MAC addresses but do not isolate devices into security zones without VLANs.
(B) Incorrect — if the entire district uses one /16 subnet, inter-building traffic stays within the same broadcast domain.
(D) Incorrect — network scanners work on any IP-connected medium, wired or wireless.
Exam Tip: Flat network = one broadcast domain = every device can see every other device. This is the fundamental problem that segmentation solves.

The IT director proposes creating five VLANs: Student (VLAN 10), Teacher (VLAN 20), Admin (VLAN 30), Guest (VLAN 40), and IoT (VLAN 50). Which of the following BEST describes the primary security benefit of this design?

VLANs create separate broadcast domains at Layer 2, confining traffic within each zone. Cross-VLAN communication requires a Layer 3 device (router or firewall), where access control policies can be enforced. This limits lateral movement — a compromised student device cannot directly reach the payroll server.
(A) Incorrect — VLANs do not encrypt traffic
column2: they create logical boundaries, not cryptographic ones.

column1: (C) Incorrect — VLANs separate traffic but inter-VLAN routing still needs firewall rules to enforce access control.
(D) Incorrect — while VLANs can reduce broadcast traffic, the primary benefit described here is security, not performance.
Exam Tip: VLANs = logical separation. Firewalls between VLANs = access control enforcement. Both are needed for effective segmentation.

After deploying VLANs, teachers on VLAN 20 need to access the SIS server on the Admin VLAN 30. Students on VLAN 10 must be blocked from the SIS entirely. Which of the following configurations achieves this?

The inter-VLAN firewall is the enforcement point. A specific ALLOW rule permits teacher VLAN traffic to reach the SIS, while a DENY rule blocks student VLAN traffic. This is precise, auditable access control between network zones.
(A) Incorrect — moving the SIS to the teacher VLAN eliminates segmentation of administrative systems and exposes the SIS to all teacher-VLAN threats.
(C) Incorrect — disabling all inter-VLAN routing would break legitimate cross-zone communication (teachers need admin resources, IoT needs management, etc.).
(D) Incorrect — merging VLANs defeats the purpose of segmentation.
Exam Tip: Inter-VLAN firewall rules follow the same principles as perimeter rules: specific ALLOWs for legitimate traffic, DENY everything else.

A security auditor discovers that several switch ports in Sycamore classrooms are configured as trunk ports (carrying traffic for all VLANs) instead of access ports (assigned to a single VLAN). Which attack does this misconfiguration enable?

Trunk ports carry tagged traffic for multiple VLANs. If an attacker connects to a misconfigured trunk port, they can send frames with 802.1Q tags for any VLAN, effectively “hopping” into VLANs they were not assigned to — such as the Admin VLAN containing payroll data.
(A) Incorrect — ARP poisoning works within a single broadcast domain and does not require trunk port access.
(C) Incorrect — DNS spoofing targets the DNS protocol, not VLAN tagging.
(D) Incorrect — trunk ports do not inherently provide more bandwidth for attack traffic.
Exam Tip: VLAN hopping prevention: configure all user-facing ports as access ports (single VLAN). Trunk ports should only connect switches to switches or to routers.

Sycamore’s 200 security cameras are placed on IoT VLAN 50 with a firewall rule allowing only outbound traffic to the camera management server (10.30.1.5) on port 554. A camera is compromised through a firmware vulnerability. Which of the following attacks is MOST effectively contained by this segmentation?

The firewall rule restricts VLAN 50 to only reaching the management server. The compromised camera cannot initiate connections to VLAN 10 (students), VLAN 20 (teachers), or VLAN 30 (admin) because the firewall blocks all cross-VLAN traffic except to the management server. Lateral movement to other VLANs is contained.
(B) Not contained — broadcast traffic stays within VLAN 50
column2: the firewall does not block intra-VLAN broadcasts.

column1: (C) Not contained — other cameras are on the same VLAN 50, so the compromised camera can reach them directly without crossing the firewall.
(D) Not contained — the firewall explicitly allows traffic to the management server on port 554.
Exam Tip: Segmentation contains lateral movement BETWEEN zones. It does not protect against attacks WITHIN the same zone. This is why micro-segmentation exists for high-security environments.
Which of the following is NOT a valid reason for placing the guest Wi-Fi on a separate VLAN from the student network?

VLANs are a Layer 2 segmentation technology — they create separate broadcast domains but do not control wireless encryption. WPA3 encryption is configured on the wireless access point, not determined by VLAN assignment. A guest VLAN could use WPA3, WPA2, or even an open network depending on AP configuration.
(A) Valid reason — unmanaged devices on a shared network can introduce malware to managed devices.
(B) Valid reason — VLAN separation + firewall rules prevent guests from reaching internal systems.
(C) Valid reason — separate VLANs allow different QoS and filtering policies per network zone.
Exam Tip: VLANs control which devices can talk to each other (segmentation). Wireless encryption controls who can join the network and protects data in transit. These are independent functions.

6 questions — Evaluate firewall configurations and packet filtering decisions

column4: >Predict the answer before selecting an option

column1: Brightpath University serves 15,000 students and 2,000 faculty across a main campus and two satellite locations. The campus network includes a student residence network, an academic research network with sensitive grant data, a public-facing web server cluster, and an administrative network handling financial aid and payroll. The IT security team is reviewing firewall policies after a recent audit flagged several misconfigurations.

Brightpath’s perimeter firewall inspects each incoming packet’s source IP, destination IP, source port, destination port, and protocol type. It does NOT track whether the packet belongs to an established connection or examine the packet’s payload. This firewall is BEST classified as:

The firewall examines header fields (IPs, ports, protocol) but does not track connection state or inspect payloads. This matches a stateless packet-filtering firewall, which evaluates each packet in isolation against its rule set.
(A) Incorrect — stateful firewalls track connection state
(B) Incorrect — NGFWs perform deep packet inspection of payloads
(D) Incorrect — WAFs are application-layer devices focused on HTTP traffic
column2: this operates at the network/transport layer.

column1: Exam Tip: Stateless = examines each packet independently (headers only). Stateful = tracks connections. NGFW = adds application awareness and deep inspection.

The following firewall rules are applied in order:

Rule 1: ALLOW TCP from 10.0.0.0/8 to ANY on port 443
Rule 2: DENY TCP from 10.0.50.0/24 to 192.168.1.100 on port 443
Rule 3: DENY ALL

A packet arrives from 10.0.50.15 destined for 192.168.1.100 on port 443. What happens to this packet?

Firewalls evaluate rules top-down and apply the first match. Rule 1 matches first because 10.0.50.15 is within the 10.0.0.0/8 range. Rule 2 never gets evaluated. This is a common misconfiguration — a broad ALLOW rule placed before a specific DENY rule renders the DENY rule useless.
(A) Incorrect — Rule 2 is never reached because Rule 1 already matches and is processed first.
(C) Incorrect — Rule 3 only applies to packets that do not match any earlier rule.
(D) Incorrect — firewalls do not default to allow on rule conflicts
Exam Tip: Firewall rule order matters. More specific rules must come BEFORE broader rules, or they will never be evaluated. This is a very common exam question format.

A student in the residence hall initiates an HTTPS connection to an external website. The outbound SYN packet is allowed by the firewall. Later, the website sends a response packet back to the student. Which of the following statements about how different firewall types handle this return traffic are correct?

I. A stateless firewall would require a separate inbound rule explicitly allowing traffic from the website’s IP to the student’s IP on the ephemeral port.
II. A stateful firewall would automatically allow the return packet because it recognizes it as part of an established TCP session.
III. A next-generation firewall would block the return packet unless the website’s domain appears on an approved application allowlist.

<div class=""fb-exp"">Statement I is correct — stateless firewalls evaluate each packet independently and cannot recognize return traffic as part of an existing session. Statement II is correct — stateful firewalls maintain a state table and automatically permit return packets for established connections. Statement III is incorrect — NGFWs include stateful tracking
column2: they would allow the return packet as part of the established session regardless of application allowlists.

column1: (A) Incomplete — Statement II is also correct.
(B) Incomplete — Statement I is also correct.
(D) Incorrect — Statement III misrepresents how NGFWs handle return traffic.
Exam Tip: Stateful firewalls solved the return-traffic problem. Without state tracking, administrators must create rules for both directions of every connection.
<div class=""q-stem"">Brightpath’s firewall policy ends with an implicit <code style=""background:#EDE9FE!important
column5: >DENY ALL rule. A new research lab needs access to an external genomics database on TCP port 8443. The IT team has not yet created a rule for this traffic. What will happen when a researcher tries to connect?

column1: A default-deny (implicit deny) policy blocks all traffic that does not match an explicit ALLOW rule. This is the most secure baseline because it requires administrators to intentionally permit each type of traffic. The connection to port 8443 will fail until the IT team creates a specific rule allowing it.
(A) Incorrect — default-deny firewalls do not make exceptions based on port similarity to known services.
(B) Incorrect — standard firewalls do not generate user-facing prompts
column2: they silently drop or reject packets.

column1: (D) Incorrect — firewalls apply rules consistently to every packet
Exam Tip: Default deny = everything is blocked unless explicitly allowed. Default allow = everything is permitted unless explicitly blocked. Default deny is the industry standard for security.

A student downloads a malware-infected PDF from a legitimate academic journal website over HTTPS. Brightpath’s stateful firewall allowed the traffic because port 443 outbound is permitted. Which limitation does this scenario demonstrate?

Standard stateful firewalls operate at Layers 3-4 (network/transport). They can track connections and filter by IP/port, but they cannot inspect the encrypted payload inside an HTTPS session. Malware inside a legitimate HTTPS download passes through because the firewall sees only the encrypted tunnel, not the file contents.
(B) Incorrect — stateful firewalls specifically track connection states
(C) Incorrect — all firewalls can filter by port number
(D) Incorrect — firewalls clearly distinguish traffic direction
column2: outbound rules are separate from inbound.

column1: Exam Tip: Encryption is a double-edged sword: it protects user privacy but also hides malicious content from network-level inspection. This is why NGFWs with TLS inspection exist.

The IT team needs to allow faculty to access the administrative payroll system (192.168.10.5, port 8080) from the academic network (172.16.0.0/16) while blocking student access from the residence network (10.10.0.0/16). Which firewall rule set achieves this with CORRECT rule ordering?

Option A correctly places the specific ALLOW for faculty first, followed by the specific DENY for students, followed by the default DENY ALL. This ensures faculty can access the system, students cannot, and all other unmatched traffic is also blocked.
(C) Incorrect — Rule 1 allows ANY source, which includes students. The student DENY in Rule 2 is never reached because Rule 1 already matched.
(D) Incorrect — Rule 2 allows ANY source after the student deny, which means any non-student IP (including guest, IoT, etc.) can access payroll.
Exam Tip: Build rules from most specific to least specific, ending with default deny. Test your rule set by tracing a packet from each source to verify correct behavior.
